slides.0.title: Geography, climate and chalk
slides.0.subtitle: A northern margin, chalk and the four sub-regions
slides.1.title: Location and a marginal northern climate
slides.1.highlights.0.title: About 150 km north-east of Paris
slides.1.highlights.0.content: The region lies at about 49°N, one of the northernmost major wine regions, with vineyards at roughly 90–300 m
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Mean annual temperature about 11°C
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Mean annual temperature is about 11°C (figures vary slightly by source). Ripening is hard, giving high acidity and modest sugar, which is what sparkling base wine needs
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Oceanic and continental influences
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Per Comité Champagne, the continental influence brings summer sun but winter frost, while the oceanic influence brings steady rain and moderate temperatures
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Vintage variation and risk
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Spring frost, mildew, hail and uneven ripening are normal at this margin, and they are why reserve wines and blending exist
slides.1.content: The logic of a marginal climate: hard ripening → high-acid base → suits second fermentation; unstable vintages → blending and reserve wines. This chain is very useful in essays.
slides.2.title: Chalk: soil, water and cellars
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Two chalk layers
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Champagne's chalk dates from the Late Cretaceous and is often divided into Belemnitella chalk and Micraster chalk, which occur at different places and depths
slides.2.highlights.1.title: A water reservoir and temperature regulator
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Per Comité Champagne chalk acts as a water reservoir and temperature regulator and is thought to contribute minerality to some wines; its porosity lets roots reach water in dry spells
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Crayères: chalk pits
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Chalk was quarried for building since antiquity, and the resulting tunnels and pits (crayères) later became wine cellars
slides.2.highlights.3.title: A cool, stable, humid ageing environment
slides.2.highlights.3.content: Cellars stretch for several hundred kilometres with a cool, stable temperature all year, ideal for lees ageing; stocks equal almost four years of shipments (over a billion bottles)
slides.2.content: Do not confuse this chalk with Chablis (Jurassic Kimmeridgian limestone-marl); use "Cretaceous versus Jurassic" when comparing the two.
slides.3.title: Administrative areas and distribution
slides.3.highlights.0.title: 3 regions, 5 départements
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Comité Champagne: the vineyard spans 3 regions, 5 départements (Marne, Aube, Aisne, Haute-Marne, Seine-et-Marne) and 319 villages
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Marne is the largest
slides.3.highlights.1.content: The Marne has by far the largest share, followed by the Aube, with the Aisne about a tenth and the Haute-Marne and Seine-et-Marne tiny
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Shares differ between sources
slides.3.highlights.2.content: A common breakdown is Marne about 66%, Aube about 23%, Aisne about 10%, yet some sources put the Marne near 75%. The official key figures give no breakdown, so we teach only the ranking and do not test the percentages
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Overall scale
slides.3.highlights.3.content: About 34,200 ha, around 4% of France's vineyard and 0.5% of the world's (Comité Champagne, consistent across the 2023–2025 editions)
slides.3.content: Level 2 will check each département's area against the latest official data; for now just build a feel for the ranking.
slides.4.title: The four sub-regions and a first look at crus
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Montagne de Reims
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Mainly Pinot Noir for structure and power, with several Grand Cru villages (covered in Level 2)
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Vallée de la Marne
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Mainly Meunier, giving round fruit and early appeal, on more varied soils
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Côte des Blancs
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Mainly Chardonnay on the purest chalk, with finesse, high acidity and longevity
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Côte des Bar (Aube)
slides.4.highlights.3.content: In the southern Aube, mainly Pinot Noir on Kimmeridgian marl, close to Chablis. Some sources list the Côte de Sézanne as a fifth sub-region
slides.4.content: Among the 319 crus, 17 villages are Grand Cru. The Premier Cru count varies by source (about 42–44) and will be checked against the official list in Level 2, so it is not tested here.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
What is chalk's key role in Champagne vineyards?
B. Acting as a water reservoir and regulating temperature
Chalk is porous, storing water and buffering temperature; it neither raises sugar nor stops frost.
The Côte des Blancs is mainly Chardonnay; the Marne Valley leans to Meunier, the Montagne de Reims and Côte des Bar to Pinot Noir.
Which département has the largest share of Champagne vineyards?
The Marne is far larger than the others (exact shares differ by source, so we do not test them).
